Day 48 of 100 · Linux Administration

apt & dnf

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished journey entry

Package managers resolve repositories, dependencies and installed state, turning software lifecycle into something the operating system can track.

Architecture / mental model

configured repositories → package metadata/dependencies → apt/dnf → installed database/files

How it works

APT is common on Debian-family systems and DNF on modern RPM-family systems. Both manage package metadata, dependency resolution, installation, upgrade and removal through distribution repositories.

Updating package metadata and upgrading installed software are distinct operations. Production patching should also account for service restarts, kernel changes and application compatibility rather than equating 'command returned 0' with 'maintenance finished.'

Package-management output and return codes matter when automation wraps these tools. A package manager may fail because of locks, repository state or dependency problems that require different responses.

Hands-on reference

sudo apt update
apt list --upgradable
sudo dnf check-update
dnf history

Verification

Inspect the installed version through the package manager and confirm the relevant service still starts and behaves correctly after an upgrade.

Field note / gotcha

Package metadata refresh and package upgrade are not the same action. Also, automation should account for package-manager return-code semantics instead of treating every non-zero code identically.

Security considerations

Use trusted repositories, verify signing configuration and patch deliberately. Removing a package should not leave a forgotten exposed service or stale credentials behind.

What I learned

Patch management is system change management, not a ritual command copied into a maintenance window.
